title: Is There No God in Israel? Elijah and Ahaziah
summary: Ahaziah, Ahab's son, is badly hurt in a fall and sends messengers to ask Baal-zebub, the god of the Philistine city of Ekron, whether he will recover. Elijah intercepts them with the LORD's verdict that the king will die. When Ahaziah sends soldiers to seize the prophet, fire from heaven consumes two companies; the third captain begs for mercy, Elijah goes to the king in person, and Ahaziah dies as the LORD had said.
story: Second Kings opens without a break from 1 Kings, which ended with Ahab dead and his son Ahaziah reigning in his place, walking in his parents' ways and serving Baal (1 Kings 22:51-53). This chapter shows what that means in practice: when the king is in trouble, he turns to a foreign god. It is also Elijah's last public act. The prophet who confronted Ahab and the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel now confronts Ahab's son with the same question, and the next chapter will tell of his departure and Elisha's succession. The note that Moab rebelled (verse 1) is left hanging and is taken up in chapter 3.
historical:
Ahaziah reigned only briefly, about 853 to 852 BC, in the years after his father's death at Ramoth-gilead. Moab, east of the Dead Sea, had been subject to Israel since Omri's day, and Ahab's death gave it the chance to break free. The Mesha Stele, a Moabite royal inscription found at Dhiban in Jordan in 1868, gives Moab's own account of that rebellion, naming Omri as the king who oppressed Moab. Ekron was one of the five chief cities of the Philistines, on the coastal plain west of Judah; its site, Tel Miqne, was confirmed in 1996 by an inscription naming the city and its rulers.

The notice in verse 17, that Jehoram of Israel succeeded Ahaziah in the second year of Jehoram son of Jehoshaphat of Judah, sits awkwardly beside 3:1, which dates the same accession to Jehoshaphat's eighteenth year. The usual explanation is a co-regency: Jehoshaphat's son Jehoram shared the throne with his father for several years before reigning alone, so the same moment could be dated by either king. The period is further confused by the fact that Israel and Judah each had a king named Jehoram (or Joram) at the same time, and soon each had an Ahaziah as well.
cultural:
Ancient kings sought oracles about illness as a matter of course, and a god with a reputation for healing or for reliable answers might draw inquirers from far away. Ahaziah's choice is telling. He does not ask the LORD, or even a local Baal in Samaria, but sends to a Philistine shrine. The name Baal-zebub means lord of flies. Many scholars think it is a deliberate Israelite mockery of the title Baal-zebul, meaning Baal the exalted or Baal the prince, a title known from the Ugaritic texts of Syria; others think it reflects a real local cult of a god who protected from flies and the disease they carried. The New Testament name Beelzebul, used of the prince of demons (Matthew 12:24), grows from this name.

Elijah's appearance is described in verse 8 as a hairy man with a leather belt, which probably refers to a garment of hair or animal skin (compare Zechariah 13:4, where a hairy cloak marks a prophet). It was the dress of someone outside the court and its comforts. The companies of fifty reflect the ordinary units of an ancient Israelite army. Summoning a prophet by armed force was an assertion that the king's command outranked the word of God, which is exactly the claim the chapter tests.
literary: The chapter is built on threes and on repetition. The LORD's question, whether it is because there is no God in Israel that the king inquires of Baal-zebub, is spoken three times: by the angel to Elijah, by the messengers to the king, and by Elijah to Ahaziah's face. Three captains come with fifty men each. The first two issue the king's command, and Elijah answers with a wordplay: if he is a man of God (ish elohim), let fire of God (esh elohim) come down. The third captain comes not with orders but on his knees, and the pattern breaks. Movement up and down carries the theme: the king will not come down from his bed, the captains order the man of God to come down, fire comes down from heaven, and finally Elijah goes down with the third captain. The closing formula in verses 17-18 marks the end of Ahaziah's reign in the book's standard style.

outline.t: Ahaziah inquires of Baal-zebub, and Elijah intercepts his messengers
Three captains and their fifties; Elijah confronts the king
Ahaziah dies according to the word of the LORD

doctrines.note: Ahaziah's sin is not only worshiping Baal but seeking life and knowledge from a god who is no god. The repeated question, “Is it because there is no God in Israel” (verse 3), shows that idolatry is at heart a refusal to trust the LORD in the moment of need.
The chapter is about where a person seeks a word. The king wants an oracle; the LORD sends one unasked, through his prophet, and it comes true exactly as spoken (verse 17).
The king's messengers, soldiers, and commands cannot touch the prophet until God permits. Power is on the hilltop with the man of God, not in the palace.

words.note: Darash, to seek, inquire, or consult. It is the regular word for asking a god or a prophet for guidance, and it appears five times here. The same verb is used when Israel is told to seek the LORD. The chapter's contrast is between seeking Baal-zebub and failing to seek the God who is present in Israel.

Baal-zebub, lord of flies, the god of Ekron. The name appears only in this chapter in the Old Testament, four times over. Whether it is a local god's real title or an Israelite parody of Baal-zebul (Baal the prince), it becomes in later Jewish and Christian usage a name for the ruler of demons.

Esh, fire. Fire from heaven recalls Mount Carmel, where the LORD answered Elijah by fire (1 Kings 18:38), and it will appear again in the chariot of fire in the next chapter. In Elijah's story fire is the sign that the LORD, not Baal, is the living God.

Se'ar, hair. The king's messengers describe the prophet literally as a lord of hair, which likely means a man wearing a hairy garment. It is enough for Ahaziah to know exactly who met them, and the description later shapes how the Gospels describe John the Baptist.

christ: Elijah's clothing in verse 8 matters for the New Testament. Matthew describes John the Baptist in a garment of camel's hair with a leather belt around his waist (Matthew 3:4), signaling that John is the Elijah whom Malachi promised would come before the day of the LORD (Malachi 4:5; Matthew 11:14). The fire from heaven also appears in the Gospels, in a telling way. When a Samaritan village refused to receive Jesus, James and John asked whether they should call down fire from heaven to consume them, and Jesus turned and rebuked them (Luke 9:51-56). The one greater than Elijah came not to destroy but to save, and he received the rejection himself. The chapter's question, whether there is no God in Israel, is answered in the Gospels by God himself dwelling among his people in the Son.

hard.q: Why did a hundred soldiers die by fire for simply obeying their king's orders?
hard.a: The deaths of the first two companies are troubling, and readers have long felt it. The text itself offers some help. The first two captains come not to inquire but to command the man of God to come down, in the name of a king who has just rejected the LORD; the second captain adds urgency to the order. The chapter presents their approach as the king's assault on the LORD's messenger, and the fire answers that challenge in the same way that fire answered the prophets of Baal on Carmel. The third captain shows that another response was possible: he humbles himself and is spared. Still, the soldiers were not the ones who sent to Ekron. Some interpreters emphasize that in the Old Testament the treatment of God's messenger is treated as the treatment of God himself, and that this was a decisive moment in the conflict with Baal worship. Others emphasize that the New Testament deliberately refuses this model: Jesus rebukes the disciples who want to repeat Elijah's fire (Luke 9:54-55). Both readings agree that the chapter is not a pattern for believers to follow.

questions: When Ahaziah was in trouble, he looked for help everywhere except to the LORD. Where do people turn first when life is threatened, and what does that reveal about what they trust?
The third captain came with a request rather than a command and was spared. What is the difference between approaching God to demand and approaching him to ask?
Jesus rebuked his disciples for wanting to call down fire like Elijah. How do you hold together a God who judges and a Savior who refused to destroy those who rejected him?
